source.title: A Neurobiological Evaluation Metric for Neural Network Model Search
source.authors: Nathaniel Blanchard; Jeffery Kinnison; Brandon RichardWebster; Pouya Bashivan; W. Scheirer

record.tranche_reason: The study measures similarity between PredNet representations and a human fMRI representation, and relates that measure to task performance. It does not test whether independently trained AI models become more similar to one another, or test any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The study's own results concern human-model similarity (HMS), not model-model convergence. Those adjacent findings are recorded with versions ["none"] and described under fits_no_version. The VLOG results are only summarized as stable across datasets; details are deferred to supplementary material not included in this text.
record.test_reason: The study's results are correlations between PredNet RDMs and one averaged human fMRI RDM (HMS), and between HMS and task performance. It never compares AI models with each other, so it cannot bear on model-model convergence (V1, V3–V7) or vision-language alignment (V2). Its only link to the claim is a citation of Li et al. (convergent learning) when it motivates the random-initialization stability test. 'Discusses' overstates this, so the relation is cites_only.
record.authors_conclusion: Essentially correct. The authors conclude that PredNets with higher similarity to the human IT fMRI RDM perform better on next-frame prediction and object matching. They add that HMS is stable across seeds, stabilizes early in training, and can serve as an early-stopping and model-search criterion, cutting training time by an estimated 67%.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses RSA to compare network and human RDMs; it does not test the original claim's model-to-model convergence method or question.

fits_no_version.finding: Across 95 PredNets, similarity to the human IT RDM correlated with task performance: rho = -0.646 with next-frame error and rho = 0.575 with object-matching accuracy. Mean HMS was 0.106, against a human-human reference of 0.19.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Within one architecture family, networks whose representations align more with human IT perform better on vision tasks (brain-model alignment rises with competence).

fits_no_version.finding: The top-ten-HMS networks had much lower prediction error (0.009) and higher accuracy (0.459) than the bottom ten (0.314 error, 0.13 accuracy).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extremes of human-model similarity track extremes of task performance in PredNets.

fits_no_version.finding: For 66 identically configured 3-layer PredNets, HMS varied little across random initializations: SD 0.02 before 100 epochs and 0.01 after.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Brain-alignment scores are stable across seeds for a fixed configuration.

fits_no_version.finding: In a larger sample (N = 1811) controlling for learning rate, the HMS-task correlations stayed significant with similar strength. Exact coefficients are not given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The HMS-performance association is not explained by learning rate.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code and data would be released following publication, but gives no URL)
record.problems: The evidence is confined to PredNet and a single averaged human fMRI RDM; the study does not compare AI models with one another or sweep model size and capability. Main-text detail for the VLOG experiments is limited, and exact partial-correlation coefficients are not given here.

untested.parts: No model-model comparison across architectures, objectives, data or scale. Only one architecture (PredNet) is compared with a brain RDM.
No vision-language or paired image-caption analysis.
Networks with different seeds are never compared with each other. Only their scores against a human RDM are compared.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation transfer between models.
No shared interpretable features or circuits across models.
Only Spearman RDM correlation on one 92-stimulus set is used. No alternative metrics or inputs are compared for model-model similarity.
No measure of how complete model-model alignment is, and no causal analysis of what drives it.

record.verdict_notes: The study is adjacent to the brain-alignment side of the Platonic Representation Hypothesis but contains no model-model comparison. The small-sample (N = 95) partial correlation controlling for learning rate was reported as not significant; only the N = 1811 repeat was significant. Row r12 should note this. VLOG cross-dataset results are in supplementary material not included here.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representations across independently trained models, architectures, objectives, data, sizes, or capability levels.
No paired image-caption vision-language comparison or cross-modal scaling analysis.
The study measures stability of HMS across random initializations, not shared features or subspaces between independently initialized networks.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment between models.
No recurring interpretable features or circuits are identified across models.
No comparison of alternative representation-similarity metrics, metric settings, or input sets for model-model convergence.
No test of whether model-model alignment is incomplete or caused by shared training data or objectives.
